chapterTitle: The Scattering That Spread the Fire
themeTitle: "When They Scattered the Church, They Only Planted It"

scripture.text: Saul was consenting to his death. A great persecution arose against the assembly which was in Jerusalem in that day. They were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except for the apostles.
scripture.understanding: The chapter opens on a funeral and a manhunt: a young Pharisee named Saul stands over Stephen's blood, approving. But watch what the persecution accidentally does — it hurls the believers out of Jerusalem into exactly the next two regions Jesus named in 1:8 (Judea and Samaria). The enemy strikes to bury the church and instead scatters its seed.

scripture.text: Devout men buried Stephen, and lamented greatly over him.
scripture.understanding: Even in a time of terror, godly men risk everything to honor a martyr's body and to grieve out loud. Their loud lament is not weak faith; it is faith brave enough to weep in public over what evil has done.

scripture.text: But Saul ravaged the assembly, entering into every house, and dragged both men and women off to prison.
scripture.understanding: The word for 'ravaged' pictures a wild animal mangling its prey — this is Saul as a one-man wrecking crew, going door to door. Remember his own name here; the man tearing the church apart is the same man Jesus is about to turn into its greatest builder.

scripture.text: Therefore those who were scattered abroad went around preaching the word.
scripture.understanding: Here is the hinge of the whole chapter. The scattered believers did not go into hiding; they went 'gossiping the gospel' everywhere they landed. Persecution did not silence the message — it distributed it.

scripture.text: Philip went down to the city of Samaria, and proclaimed to them the Christ.
scripture.understanding: This is Philip the deacon (Acts 6:5), not the apostle. He crosses the oldest hatred in Israel — Jews despised Samaritans — and heralds Christ to them. The gospel's first great barrier falls here, and it is a table-waiter, not an apostle, who breaks through.

scripture.text: The multitudes listened with one accord to the things that were spoken by Philip, when they heard and saw the signs which he did.
scripture.understanding: A whole city leans in together. The signs were not the message — they were the confirmation that authenticated the message so the Samaritans would hear the word about Christ.

scripture.text: For unclean spirits came out of many of those who had them. They came out, crying with a loud voice. Many who had been paralyzed and lame were healed.
scripture.understanding: The kingdom of God collides with the kingdom of darkness in Samaria, and darkness loses loudly — demons scream as they are evicted. Bodies long bound to paralysis stand up free. Jesus is still doing by His Spirit what He began to do in the Gospels.

scripture.text: There was great joy in that city.
scripture.understanding: One short sentence carries the whole result. Where Christ is preached and darkness is driven out, the atmosphere over a place changes from oppression to joy.

scripture.text: But there was a certain man, Simon by name, who used to practice sorcery in the city, and amazed the people of Samaria, making himself out to be some great one,
scripture.understanding: Enter the counterfeit. Before Philip came, Simon had the whole city under a spell of amazement, and the center of his 'ministry' was himself — 'making himself out to be some great one.' Watch the contrast: Philip exalts Christ; Simon exalts Simon.

scripture.text: to whom they all listened, from the least to the greatest, saying, “This man is that great power of God.”
scripture.understanding: The whole social ladder, top to bottom, was captivated. They even attached God's name to Simon's power — the oldest lie, calling a man's counterfeit 'the great power of God.'

scripture.text: They listened to him, because for a long time he had amazed them with his sorceries.
scripture.understanding: Simon's grip was built on time and spectacle — 'a long time' of amazing them. But amazement is not conversion; a crowd stunned by wonders can still have a heart untouched by God.

scripture.text: But when they believed Philip preaching good news concerning God’s Kingdom and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women.
scripture.understanding: The little word 'But' shatters Simon's spell. The content of true gospel preaching is named exactly: the Kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ. Belief led straight to public baptism, for men and women alike.

scripture.text: Simon himself also believed. Being baptized, he continued with Philip. Seeing signs and great miracles occurring, he was amazed.
scripture.understanding: Even Simon 'believed' and was baptized — but notice what still holds his heart: he is 'amazed,' the same reaction he once produced in others. The manipulator who dazzled the city is now the one dazzled. It reads like conversion, but the coming verses expose a heart never truly bent to God.

scripture.text: Now when the apostles who were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them,
scripture.understanding: The Jerusalem apostles do not ignore Samaria's harvest — they authenticate it. Sending Peter and John (John, who once wanted to call fire down on a Samaritan village, Luke 9:54) is itself a miracle of grace.

scripture.text: who, when they had come down, prayed for them, that they might receive the Holy Spirit;
scripture.understanding: The apostles' first act is not to inspect but to pray — that these new Samaritan believers would receive the Holy Spirit Himself, the very center of the whole book of Acts.

scripture.text: for as yet he had fallen on none of them. They had only been baptized in the name of Christ Jesus.
scripture.understanding: God deliberately delayed the Spirit's coming until the Jerusalem apostles arrived, so that Samaritan believers and Jewish believers would be visibly joined into one church under one Spirit — no rival, separate Samaritan Christianity. Unity in the Spirit is the point.

scripture.text: Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.
scripture.understanding: Through the laying on of the apostles' hands, the Samaritans receive the Spirit — the same Pentecost gift now crossing an ancient racial wall. Something visible and unmistakable happened here, because Simon saw it and coveted it.

scripture.text: Now when Simon saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money,
scripture.understanding: Here is the moment that named a sin forever — 'simony,' trying to buy the things of God. Simon's old operating system surfaces: he sees spiritual power as a product to be purchased and resold.

scripture.text: saying, “Give me also this power, that whomever I lay my hands on may receive the Holy Spirit.”
scripture.understanding: Notice what he wants and does not want: he asks for the power to dispense the Spirit, not for the Spirit to master him. He wants God's gift as a tool for his own greatness, exactly as he wanted his sorceries.

scripture.text: But Peter said to him, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money!
scripture.understanding: Peter's rebuke is thunder, not diplomacy. The 'gift of God' cannot be bought precisely because it is a gift — to price it is to insult the Giver. And Peter warns that the money and the man who trusts it will perish together.

scripture.text: You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart isn’t right before God.
scripture.understanding: Peter cuts past the baptism and the outward belief to the real issue: the heart. A crooked heart can go through every religious motion and still have 'neither part nor lot' in the things of God.

scripture.text: Repent therefore of this, your wickedness, and ask God if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you.
scripture.understanding: Even to a man this far gone, the door of repentance is open. Peter names the disease (wickedness of heart) and prescribes the only cure — turn, and ask God for mercy on the very thought.

scripture.text: For I see that you are in the poison of bitterness and in the bondage of iniquity.”
scripture.understanding: Peter's Spirit-given discernment sees straight through the baptismal water into Simon's soul: he is soaked in 'poison of bitterness' and chained by 'the bondage of iniquity.' The outward profession never freed the inward captivity.

scripture.text: Simon answered, “Pray for me to the Lord, that none of the things which you have spoken happen to me.”
scripture.understanding: Simon fears the penalty but never repents of the sin. He asks Peter to pray the consequences away, like a man dreading the sentence yet unwilling to leave the crime. Scripture leaves him there, a sober warning that trembling at judgment is not the same as turning to God.

scripture.text: They therefore, when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, returned to Jerusalem, and preached the Good News to many villages of the Samaritans.
scripture.understanding: The apostles do not merely visit one city and leave — on the way home they evangelize many Samaritan villages. The wall between Jew and Samaritan is not just crossed; it is being torn down village by village.

scripture.text: But an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, “Arise, and go toward the south to the way that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza. This is a desert.”
scripture.understanding: God pulls His best evangelist out of a booming citywide revival and sends him to a lonely desert road. Heaven's math is different from ours: the Spirit will leave the crowd for the sake of one seeking soul.

scripture.text: He arose and went; and behold, there was a man of Ethiopia, a eunuch of great authority under Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was over all her treasure, who had come to Jerusalem to worship.
scripture.understanding: Philip's instant obedience meets a divine appointment: a high African official — treasurer of a queen — a God-fearing worshiper who had traveled hundreds of miles to Jerusalem. As a eunuch he could never fully enter the temple (Deuteronomy 23:1); he came to worship a God whose house kept him at the edge.

scripture.text: He was returning and sitting in his chariot, and was reading the prophet Isaiah.
scripture.understanding: A hungry heart on the long road home, reading aloud from a costly scroll of Isaiah. God had already prepared the soil; Philip is being sent to a man mid-sentence in the exact scripture that points to Jesus.

scripture.text: The Spirit said to Philip, “Go near, and join yourself to this chariot.”
scripture.understanding: The angel got Philip to the road; now the Holy Spirit gives the precise, moment-by-moment instruction: 'Go near.' The true Director of this whole book speaks directly to His servant's ear.

scripture.text: Philip ran to him, and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet, and said, “Do you understand what you are reading?”
scripture.understanding: Philip runs — obedience with urgency — and opens with a question, not a lecture. He meets the man exactly where he already is, in the pages of Isaiah, and asks the doorway question every teacher should ask.

scripture.text: He said, “How can I, unless someone explains it to me?” He begged Philip to come up and sit with him.
scripture.understanding: Here is the humble hunger God loves — a powerful man admitting he cannot understand alone and begging for a guide. This is why teachers exist: God ordinarily opens the Scriptures to the seeker through a sent explainer.

scripture.text: Now the passage of the Scripture which he was reading was this, “He was led as a sheep to the slaughter. As a lamb before his shearer is silent, so he doesn’t open his mouth.
scripture.understanding: Of all the scrolls, of all the chapters, the eunuch was reading Isaiah 53 — the suffering Servant, silent as a lamb going to the slaughter. God arranged the timing so that the man was staring at the very prophecy of the cross when the preacher of the cross arrived.

scripture.text: In his humiliation, his judgment was taken away. Who will declare His generation? For his life is taken from the earth.”
scripture.understanding: The Servant is humiliated, denied justice, His life cut off from the earth — Isaiah wrote it seven centuries before Calvary. The eunuch is holding the fingerprint of the crucifixion and does not yet know whose face it is.

scripture.text: The eunuch answered Philip, “Who is the prophet talking about? About himself, or about someone else?”
scripture.understanding: The perfect question, asked by an honest seeker. He knows the text is about a person; he simply needs the name. That name is the whole missing key.

scripture.text: Philip opened his mouth, and beginning from this Scripture, preached to him about Jesus.
scripture.understanding: Starting from Isaiah 53, Philip preaches Jesus — proof that the Old Testament, rightly opened, leads straight to Christ. He does not change the subject; he reveals the subject. The silent Lamb has a name, and His name is Jesus.

scripture.text: As they went on the way, they came to some water, and the eunuch said, “Behold, here is water. What is keeping me from being baptized?”
scripture.understanding: The moment he understands, he wants to belong publicly. The man who was once barred from the temple asks the question of a truly welcomed son: 'What is keeping me from being baptized?' In Christ, the answer is nothing.

This verse is blank in the World English Bible on purpose. The words traditionally numbered 37 — the eunuch's confession, 'I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God' — are absent from the oldest and most reliable Greek manuscripts and were added by later scribes, so modern translations honestly leave the slot empty. The truth it states is right; its place in the original text is not certain.

scripture.text: He commanded the chariot to stand still, and they both went down into the water, both Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him.
scripture.understanding: The treasurer of a queen halts his whole caravan for the sake of obeying Christ. Both men go down into the water together — a picture of full immersion and of a barrier permanently gone.

scripture.text: When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught Philip away, and the eunuch didn’t see him any more, for he went on his way rejoicing.
scripture.understanding: The Spirit who directed the whole encounter now sweeps Philip away, his mission with this man complete. The eunuch does not chase the preacher — he goes on his way 'rejoicing,' carrying the gospel toward Africa. He came to worship at a distance and leaves as a baptized son, full of joy.

scripture.text: But Philip was found at Azotus. Passing through, he preached the Good News to all the cities, until he came to Caesarea.
scripture.understanding: Philip resurfaces up the coast at Azotus and simply keeps doing what he always does — preaching the Good News in every city all the way to Caesarea. The scattered seed is now scattering itself; the fire cannot be contained.

visualMeditations.title: The Scattered Seed
visualMeditations.image: Picture a farmer's hand plunging into a sack and flinging grain across a wide field — the seeds fly in every direction, landing far from where they started. That is exactly the Greek picture in verse 1: the believers were diaspeirō-ed, 'sown throughout.' The soldiers and Saul think they are stamping out a fire in Jerusalem, but every believer they chase out of the city is a burning ember carried on the wind to a new region — and wherever an ember lands, it starts a new blaze of preaching (v. 4).
visualMeditations.meaning: The very weapon meant to destroy the church became the method that spread it. Persecution did not scatter the church into extinction; it planted the church across Judea and Samaria — fulfilling Jesus' words in Acts 1:8 by force. What the enemy means for burial, God means for sowing.

visualMeditations.title: The City Under Two Spells
visualMeditations.image: See Samaria as a city that had been hypnotized for years. Simon the sorcerer stood at its center like a stage magician who never left the stage, and the whole population — 'from the least to the greatest' — stood slack-jawed, calling him 'the great power of God.' Then Philip walks in, and a different power moves: demons flee screaming, paralyzed legs straighten, and the amazement that once pointed at Simon turns into joy that points at Christ. Even Simon himself is left standing in the crowd, dazzled by a power he cannot fake.
visualMeditations.meaning: There are two kinds of wonder in this chapter: the amazement a manipulator produces to exalt himself, and the joy the gospel produces to exalt Christ. A crowd can be spellbound and still be lost. Only the word about the Kingdom and the name of Jesus produces the real thing — believing hearts and public baptism.

visualMeditations.title: The Coin Held Up to Heaven
visualMeditations.image: Freeze the frame on Simon's outstretched hand — palm open, silver coins glinting in it, held up toward Peter as if the Holy Spirit were a franchise to be purchased. Then hear Peter's voice crack like thunder over that little pile of money: 'May your silver perish with you!' Imagine the coins suddenly looking like exactly what they are — worthless slugs held up against the priceless gift of God.
visualMeditations.meaning: Simon looked at the power of God and saw a business opportunity. Peter's rebuke exposes the deepest heart-sin of religion: treating God as a means to my own greatness. The gift of God (dōrea) is a gift by definition — the moment you try to pay for it, you prove you never understood grace at all.

visualMeditations.title: The Chariot Stopped in the Desert
visualMeditations.image: A dusty desert road under a hard sun. A gleaming royal chariot rolls south, and inside it a foreign dignitary is reading aloud, his finger moving under the words of a lamb led to slaughter. A man on foot runs alongside the wheels — Philip — and calls up, 'Do you understand what you are reading?' The great man does something great men rarely do: he reaches down, pulls the stranger up beside him, and says, 'How can I, unless someone explains it to me?' Miles later the chariot lurches to a halt beside a pool of water, and two men wade in together.
visualMeditations.meaning: God will move heaven and angels and His own Spirit to reach one hungry heart holding an open Bible. The eunuch had the right scroll open to the right chapter but no one to explain it — so God sent an explainer. This is the pattern of all discipleship: a seeker humble enough to say 'I can't understand alone,' and a servant obedient enough to run to the chariot.

structure.label: The Persecution and the Scattering (v. 1-4)
structure.body: Saul's assault drives the church out of Jerusalem — and the scattered believers preach everywhere they go.

structure.label: Revival in Samaria (v. 5-8)
structure.body: Philip proclaims Christ, demons flee, the sick are healed, and a whole city fills with joy.

structure.label: Simon the Sorcerer Believes (v. 9-13)
structure.body: The city's counterfeit wonder-worker is eclipsed by the real power of the gospel and is himself baptized.

structure.label: The Apostles and the Spirit (v. 14-17)
structure.body: Peter and John come down and the Samaritans receive the Holy Spirit, binding them into the one church.

structure.label: The Sin of Simony Rebuked (v. 18-24)
structure.body: Simon tries to buy the Spirit's power; Peter exposes his unrepentant heart and calls him to repent.

structure.label: The Ethiopian Eunuch (v. 25-39)
structure.body: The Spirit sends Philip to a desert road to open Isaiah 53 to a seeking African official, who believes and is baptized.

structure.label: Philip Keeps Preaching (v. 40)
structure.body: Caught away by the Spirit, Philip continues evangelizing every city up the coast to Caesarea.

sections.heading: The Strategy Hidden Inside the Suffering
paragraphs: Acts 8 is the chapter where the church's darkest day becomes its greatest advance. In 1:8 the risen Jesus had laid out the map — Jerusalem, then Judea and Samaria, then the ends of the earth. But for seven chapters the church stayed comfortably in Jerusalem. It took a great persecution to unstick them. The very violence that killed Stephen and jailed men and women is the wind that carries the seed to exactly the next zones on Jesus' map. Luke wants us to see that no weapon formed against the church can do anything but serve the church's mission.

This is the honest, un-sentimental truth of the truth: God did not merely comfort the church in its suffering — He used the suffering as His delivery system. The scattered ones 'went around preaching the word' (v. 4). They were not professional missionaries; they were ordinary refugees who could not stop talking about Jesus. The gospel spreads fastest not from the top down through institutions but from the ground up through scattered, ordinary, burning believers.

sections.heading: Real Belief and Its Counterfeit
paragraphs: The two halves of the chapter hold up two very different 'believers.' Simon the sorcerer 'believed' and was baptized (v. 13), yet Peter later declares his heart 'isn't right before God' and that he is still 'in the poison of bitterness and in the bondage of iniquity' (v. 21, 23). The Ethiopian eunuch believed and was baptized (v. 36-38) and went on his way rejoicing. Same outward steps — profession and water — but opposite hearts.

The dividing line is not the ritual; it is what the person wanted. Simon wanted the power of God as a tool to exalt Simon — he asked to be able to dispense the Spirit, never to be mastered by Him. The eunuch wanted the Christ of the Scripture and asked only, 'What is keeping me from being baptized?' Acts 8 refuses to let us equate baptism with conversion or amazement with faith. God looks past the water to the wanting of the heart. That is a sobering mirror: it is entirely possible to be baptized, to be near the miracles, even to be 'amazed,' and to have neither part nor lot in the matter because the heart was never truly surrendered.

sections.heading: The Gospel Crosses Every Wall
paragraphs: Structurally, Acts 8 is the great barrier-breaking chapter. First the gospel crosses the racial-religious wall between Jew and Samaritan — the oldest, bitterest divide in the land, a hatred centuries deep — and God deliberately withholds the Spirit until the Jerusalem apostles arrive, so that there can be no separate, rival Samaritan church. One Christ, one Spirit, one people. Then the gospel crosses to the Ethiopian eunuch: a Gentile, a foreigner from the ends of the known earth, and a man whose physical condition had kept him at the very edge of the temple courts (Deuteronomy 23:1). The man the old covenant kept at a distance, the new covenant welcomes fully into the water. Acts 8 is God announcing in advance that in Christ there is no wall — not of race, not of nation, not of the shame that once shut you out.

ntConnection.heading: New Testament Connection
paragraphs: The center of this chapter is the eunuch reading Isaiah 53:7-8, quoted in verses 32-33: 'He was led as a sheep to the slaughter... his life is taken from the earth.' The eunuch's question — 'Who is the prophet talking about?' — is answered by the entire New Testament. Philip 'beginning from this Scripture, preached to him about Jesus' (v. 35), and the apostolic church would forever read Isaiah's silent, slaughtered Lamb as Jesus of Nazareth. Peter makes the identification explicit in 1 Peter 2:22-24, quoting the same passage: Christ 'committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth... who his own self bore our sins in his body on the tree.' John the Baptist had already pointed and said, 'Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!' (John 1:29). Acts 8 is the moment the church's foundational reading of the cross — Jesus as Isaiah's suffering Servant — is preached to the first African convert, from the very chapter that prophesied it seven hundred years before Calvary.

lexicon.insight: Built from dia ('throughout') and speirō ('to sow seed'), this word literally means 'to sow throughout' — it is the root of the word 'diaspora.' Luke did not have to call the persecution a scattering of seed, but he chose the farming word on purpose. The believers were not blown away like ash; they were flung out like grain over a field. Every place a persecuted believer landed became new soil for the gospel. This single verb is the theology of the whole chapter: what looks like the church being destroyed is really the church being planted.

From eu ('good') and angellō ('to announce'), this is the verb for spilling out good news — it gives us 'evangelize.' It threads through the whole chapter: the scattered ones do it everywhere (v. 4), Philip does it about the Kingdom and the name of Jesus (v. 12), he does it to one man from Isaiah 53 (v. 35), and he does it in every city on the coast (v. 40). Notice the range — from a whole city to a single seeker in a chariot. Evangelism in Acts is not a program; it is what ordinary Spirit-filled people cannot stop doing wherever the wind sets them down.

Pneuma means 'breath, wind, spirit' — the same word Jesus used in John 3 for the wind that 'blows where it wants.' In Acts 8 the Holy Spirit is not a topic; He is the active Director of every scene. He is received by the Samaritans (v. 17), coveted by Simon (v. 18), speaks directly to Philip on the road (v. 29), and finally catches Philip away (v. 39). Acts is 'the Acts of the Holy Spirit,' and this chapter proves it — the wind that scattered the church also drives one man to a lonely desert road for the sake of one seeking soul.

Mageía (from the same root as magos, the 'wise men' of Matthew 2) is manipulative magic — power used to control people and exalt the practitioner. It is the deliberate counterfeit of the chapter. Simon's mageía 'amazed' the whole city and made him seem to be 'the great power of God,' but it produced no repentance, no cleansing, no joy — only slack-jawed dependence on the man. Held next to Philip's Spirit-power, mageía is exposed as spectacle without salvation. The chapter draws a hard line: true power drives out demons and fills a city with joy; counterfeit power just keeps the crowd amazed at you.

Dōreá means a free gratuity — a present, something given, never earned or bought. Peter drives his whole rebuke of Simon into this one word: 'you thought you could obtain the gift (dōreá) of God with money!' The very grammar of grace makes simony impossible. If the Spirit could be purchased, He would be a wage, not a gift; if He could be sold, grace would be merchandise. The moment Simon reached for his silver, he proved he had never grasped that everything God gives is dōreá — free, or not from God at all.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: The Spirit is dealing with what you do with disruption, what your heart really wants from God, and whether you will move for the sake of one soul.

items.title: What Scattered You Was Meant to Send You
items.body: The believers did not choose to leave Jerusalem — they were driven out, uprooted, dislocated by force. And in the very place the persecution dumped them, they preached. Think about the disruption in your own life: the job you lost, the city you had to move to, the plan that fell apart, the season that scattered you. The Spirit asks a piercing question — have you spent that displacement complaining, or have you preached where you landed? What if the thing that scattered you is the very thing God used to send you? Are you treating your disruption as a burial or as a sowing?

items.title: The Coin in Your Hand
items.body: Simon is a mirror held up to religious ambition. He had been baptized, he had seen the miracles, he was near everything holy — and his heart was still crooked, because he wanted God's power as a tool for his own greatness. Ask the Spirit to search you here: do you want God, or do you want what God can do for your platform, your reputation, your influence? Do you serve to be surrendered, or to be seen as 'some great one'? The most frightening line in the chapter is Peter's — 'you have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart isn't right before God' — spoken to a baptized believer. Is there a coin in your hand you are quietly holding up to heaven, trying to trade for greatness?

items.title: Will You Leave the Crowd for the One?
items.body: Philip was in the middle of a citywide revival — crowds, miracles, joy — when the angel sent him to an empty desert road for a single man. Heaven's economy will pull you out of the spotlight for the sake of one hungry soul. The eunuch was reading the right scripture and drowning in it alone, begging, 'How can I, unless someone explains it to me?' There is a person like that within your reach right now — reading, searching, one honest conversation away from Christ. Will you run to the chariot? Are you willing to be inconvenient, to be redirected, to leave the crowd for the one God has already prepared?

audit.title: The Scattering Check
audit.body: What disruption in your life have you been treating as a curse — a burial? Have you preached, served, and loved where God scattered you, or have you spent that season only trying to get back to your old 'Jerusalem'?

audit.title: The Simon Check
audit.body: Be brutally honest: is there a place where you want God's power or blessing more than you want God Himself? Where are you trying to use the things of God to make yourself 'some great one' rather than to make Him great?

audit.title: The Chariot Check
audit.body: Who is the one person in your life right now who is quietly searching — reading, asking, hungry — and has no one to explain it to them? Have you run to that chariot, or have you been too busy with the crowd to notice the one?

practices.title: Preach Where You Were Scattered
practices.body: Name one hard place life has put you — a workplace, a family situation, a city you didn't choose. This week, do one deliberate act of gospel witness right there: a conversation, an invitation, an unmistakable act of Christlike love. Treat the very place you resent as the field God sowed you into.

practices.title: Run to One Chariot
practices.body: Identify by name one seeking person within your reach. Before the week is out, sit down with them and ask a Philip-question: 'Do you understand what you're reading / what you believe / who Jesus is?' Then, beginning from wherever they are, point them to Jesus. Do not wait for them to find a teacher — be the one God sends.

prayerReflection: "Father, thank You that no weapon formed against Your church can do anything but serve Your mission. When the enemy scattered them, You only planted them — so teach me to see my own disruptions as Your sowing, not my burial. Let me preach the Good News wherever You set me down. Search my heart the way You searched Simon's; expose any place where I want Your power more than I want You, any coin I am secretly holding up to heaven for my own greatness. Cleanse me of the poison of bitterness and the bondage of iniquity, and give me a heart that is right before You. Holy Spirit, You who spoke to Philip on the desert road, speak to me — make me quick to obey, willing to leave the crowd for the one. Show me the chariot You have already prepared, and let me run to it. And like the eunuch, when I have met the Lamb of Isaiah 53 afresh, let me go on my way rejoicing. In Jesus' name, Amen."

storyConnections.title: Joseph: What the Brothers Meant for Evil
storyConnections.summary: Joseph's brothers threw him in a pit and sold him into slavery, meaning to destroy him and his dreams. Instead, God used that very betrayal to place Joseph in Egypt exactly where he needed to be to save nations from famine. Standing before the brothers years later, Joseph names the pattern: 'You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.' Acts 8 is that verse written on a bigger canvas — the persecution meant to bury the church is the very thing God used to spread it across Judea and Samaria. The scattering was the sending.

storyConnections.title: Jesus and the Samaritan Woman
storyConnections.summary: Years before Philip went to Samaria, Jesus deliberately traveled through it and stopped at a well to speak with a Samaritan woman — crossing the same ancient wall of hatred. He revealed Himself to her as the Messiah, and she ran to tell her whole town, so that 'many of the Samaritans believed.' Jesus told His disciples the fields were already 'white for harvest.' In Acts 8 that harvest comes in: Philip reaps in Samaria what Jesus had sown, and a whole city that once received a woman's testimony now receives the preaching of Christ with joy.

storyConnections.title: The Foreigner and the Eunuch Isaiah Promised
storyConnections.summary: In the Law, a eunuch was excluded from the assembly of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:1). But Isaiah 56 held out a stunning promise: the day would come when God would say to the eunuch who holds fast His covenant, 'I will give them an everlasting name that will not be cut off,' and He would gather the foreigner to Himself. In Acts 8 that prophecy walks up a desert road in a chariot. An Ethiopian eunuch — a foreigner and a eunuch, doubly excluded under the old order — hears the gospel from Isaiah's own scroll, is baptized fully into the people of God, and goes on his way rejoicing. The man the temple kept at the edge, Christ welcomed all the way in.
